claims.text: Partially replacing heavy refractory elements with lighter elements such as Al or Ti lowers the overall density of a high-entropy alloy.
A lightweight-element-modified high-entropy alloy can provide superior comprehensive performance.
Conventional HEAs based on Mo, Nb, Ta, and W have high density.
Conventional HEAs based on Mo, Nb, Ta, and W have excellent high-temperature strength.
Multi-principal-element HEAs exhibit lattice-distortion and cocktail effects.
The multicomponent nature of HEAs is associated with unusual phase or microstructural stability.
Introducing lightweight elements modifies atomic packing in a refractory HEA.
Lightweight-element substitution can modify atomic packing without sacrificing solid-solution strength.
Interactions among multiple principal elements can produce a balance of strength, ductility, and oxidation resistance.
HEAs can exhibit high strength, corrosion resistance, oxidation resistance, and thermal or microstructural stability.
Replacing heavy atoms with lighter atoms increases the alloy's specific strength.
The lightweight-modified HEA retains favorable mechanical properties relative to a conventional heavy-element HEA.
The lightweight-modified HEA retains favorable corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to a conventional heavy-element HEA.
The benefits of lightweight-modified HEAs are especially relevant to aerospace and advanced-energy applications where weight reduction is important.
At extreme temperatures, removal of heavy elements may impair phase stability because those elements contribute to stability.
The effects of exact lightweight-element substitution ratios on phase stability, microstructure evolution, and long-term performance are not fully established.
